generatedProse.concept-context: Familiarise yourself with your coaching module's outcomes before you do anything else. Make notes on them. Each one uses a verb that signals the kind of performance expected, whether that is to describe a drill, to apply a coaching model, to analyse a training session or to evaluate how well a session plan met its aims. That verb is a strong clue to how the assessment will be marked. Checking your work against the outcomes as you go is a quick way to see whether you are doing what the module actually asks, because assessment in sport coaching is intentionally aligned to those outcomes.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students read the same learning outcome from their module handbook: Evaluate the effectiveness of a session plan for developing passing under pressure.

Tom reads it quickly and starts describing the session: what the drills are, how they are set up, how long each one runs. The writing is accurate, but it only describes. The outcome asked for something the writing never does.

Amara reads the same outcome and breaks it down first. The verb is evaluate, which means weighing strengths against weaknesses to reach a judgement. What it is about is the session's effectiveness for passing under pressure specifically, not simply how the drills work. Demonstrating it means reaching a reasoned view, backed by evidence from the session, about when the plan builds that skill and when it does not, for example when a drill stays too unopposed to transfer. Amara then writes to exactly that.

Both students know the drills. Only Amara answered the outcome, because only Amara worked out what it was asking.
generatedProse.summary: Learning outcomes state what each module in the School of Sport expects you to be able to do, and they are where your assessment points, by design. You can now find the outcomes in your own module's documentation, and break one down into its active verb and what it asks you to demonstrate. Reading outcomes this way turns a vague aim into a clear target, which matters in a field where describing a session and evaluating it earn very different marks.

check.body: You are breaking down a sport coaching learning outcome that begins with the verb 'analyse'. Which of these shows you have understood what that verb asks for?

items.text: Separating the session or performance data into their parts, examining how they relate, and saying what that shows.
Listing everything you can remember about the topic.
Giving your personal opinion of the session.
Describing the session clearly from start to finish.

feedback.correct: That's right. To analyse is to break something into its parts, examine how they relate, and say what that shows, which is more than listing, opinion or description.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what 'analyse' asks for that listing, opinion or description do not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: To analyse is to separate the session or performance data into their parts, examine how they relate, and say what that shows. Listing, giving an opinion and describing are each doing something the verb does not ask for.
